item.text:
Rain forms as water moves through a continuous cycle between Earth’s surface and the atmosphere. Heat from the Sun warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground. Some of this liquid water changes into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. Plants also release water vapor from their leaves, adding moisture to the atmosphere.

As moist air rises, it encounters lower air pressure and expands. Expansion makes the air cool. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor as warmer air, so when it cools enough, some vapor changes back into tiny liquid droplets. This change is called condensation. The droplets gather around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, or smoke. A vast number of these droplets form a cloud. Clouds are made of water droplets, ice crystals, or a mixture of both; they are not masses of water vapor.

Inside a cloud, droplets move with currents of rising and falling air. They collide and join together, gradually growing larger. In cold clouds, ice crystals can grow by drawing water vapor from nearby droplets. The crystals may also collide with droplets and become coated in ice. When they grow heavy enough, they begin to fall. If they pass through air that is warmer than freezing, they melt into raindrops before reaching the ground. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or other forms of frozen precipitation.

Raindrops do not usually begin as tiny, perfectly formed teardrops. Small droplets are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. As they fall and meet air resistance, larger drops flatten at the bottom. Very large drops become unstable and break apart into smaller ones, limiting how big a falling raindrop can get.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on conditions beneath the cloud. Falling drops may evaporate in dry air, leaving a streak called virga. If enough water survives the descent, it reaches the surface as rain. Wind can carry the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the cloud’s center.

After rain reaches the ground, it may soak into soil, collect in streams and lakes, or flow across the land into rivers and eventually the sea. Some returns to the air through evaporation or plant release. The cycle then continues: water rises, cools, condenses into clouds, and may fall again as precipitation.

If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or other forms of frozen precipitation.

Rain forms as water moves through a continuous cycle between Earth’s surface and the atmosphere. Heat from the Sun warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground. Some of this liquid water changes into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. Plants also release water vapor from their leaves, adding moisture to the atmosphere.

As moist air rises, it encounters lower air pressure and expands. Expansion makes the air cool. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor as warmer air, so when it cools enough, some vapor changes back into tiny liquid droplets. This change is called condensation. The droplets gather around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, or smoke. A vast number of these droplets form a cloud. Clouds are made of water droplets, ice crystals, or a mixture of both; they are not masses of water vapor.

Inside a cloud, droplets move with currents of rising and falling air. They collide and join together, gradually growing larger. In cold clouds, ice crystals can grow by drawing water vapor from nearby droplets. The crystals may also collide with droplets and become coated in ice. When they grow heavy enough, they begin to fall. If they pass through air that is warmer than freezing, they melt into raindrops before reaching the ground. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or other forms of frozen precipitation.

Rain forms as water moves through a continuous cycle between Earth’s surface and the atmosphere. Heat from the Sun warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground. Some of this liquid water changes into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. Plants also release water vapor from their leaves, adding moisture to the atmosphere.

As moist air rises, it encounters lower air pressure and expands. Expansion makes the air cool. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor as warmer air, so when it cools enough, some vapor changes back into tiny liquid droplets. This change is called condensation. The droplets gather around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, or smoke. A vast number of these droplets form a cloud. Clouds are made of water droplets, ice crystals, or a mixture of both; they are not masses of water vapor.

Inside a cloud, droplets move with currents of rising and falling air. They collide and join together, gradually growing larger. In cold clouds, ice crystals can grow by drawing water vapor from nearby droplets. The crystals may also collide with droplets and become coated in ice. When they grow heavy enough, they begin to fall. If they pass through air that is warmer than freezing, they melt into raindrops before reaching the ground. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or other forms of frozen precipitation.

Rain forms as water moves through a continuous cycle between Earth’s surface and the atmosphere. Heat from the Sun warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground. Some of this liquid water changes into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. Plants also release water vapor from their leaves, adding moisture to the atmosphere.

As moist air rises, it encounters lower air pressure and expands. Expansion makes the air cool. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor as warmer air, so when it cools enough, some vapor changes back into tiny liquid droplets. This change is called condensation. The droplets gather around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, or smoke. A vast number of these droplets form a cloud. Clouds are made of water droplets, ice crystals, or a mixture of both; they are not masses of water vapor.

Inside a cloud, droplets move with currents of rising and falling air. They collide and join together, gradually growing larger. In cold clouds, ice crystals can grow by drawing water vapor from nearby droplets. The crystals may also collide with droplets and become coated in ice. When they grow heavy enough, they begin to fall. If they pass through air that is warmer than freezing, they melt into raindrops before reaching the ground. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or other forms of frozen precipitation.

Rain forms as water moves through a continuous cycle between Earth’s surface and the atmosphere. Heat from the Sun warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground. Some of this liquid water changes into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. Plants also release water vapor from their leaves, adding moisture to the atmosphere.

As moist air rises, it encounters lower air pressure and expands. Expansion makes the air cool. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor as warmer air, so when it cools enough, some vapor changes back into tiny liquid droplets. This change is called condensation. The droplets gather around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, or smoke. A vast number of these droplets form a cloud. Clouds are made of water droplets, ice crystals, or a mixture of both; they are not masses of water vapor.

Inside a cloud, droplets move with currents of rising and falling air. They collide and join together, gradually growing larger. In cold clouds, ice crystals can grow by drawing water vapor from nearby droplets. The crystals may also collide with droplets and become coated in ice. When they grow heavy enough, they begin to fall. If they pass through air that is warmer than freezing, they melt into raindrops before reaching the ground. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or other forms of frozen precipitation.

Some of this liquid water changes into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. Plants also release water vapor from their leaves, adding moisture to the atmosphere.

As moist air rises, it encounters lower air pressure and expands. Expansion makes the air cool. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor as warmer air, so when it cools enough, some vapor changes back into tiny liquid droplets. This change is called condensation. The droplets gather around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, or smoke. A vast number of these droplets form a cloud. Clouds are made of water droplets, ice crystals, or a mixture of both; they are not masses of water vapor.

Inside a cloud, droplets move with currents of rising and falling air. They collide and join together, gradually growing larger. In cold clouds, ice crystals can grow by drawing water vapor from nearby droplets. The crystals may also collide with droplets and become coated in ice. When they grow heavy enough, they begin to fall. If they pass through air that is warmer than freezing, they melt into raindrops before reaching the ground. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or other forms of frozen precipitation.

Raindrops do not usually begin as tiny, perfectly formed teardrops. Small droplets are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. As they fall and meet air resistance, larger drops flatten at the bottom. Very large drops become unstable and break apart into smaller ones, limiting how big a falling raindrop can get.

The droplets gather around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, or smoke. A vast number of these droplets form a cloud. Clouds are made of water droplets, ice crystals, or a mixture of both; they are not masses of water vapor.

Inside a cloud, droplets move with currents of rising and falling air. They collide and join together, gradually growing larger. In cold clouds, ice crystals can grow by drawing water vapor from nearby droplets. The crystals may also collide with droplets and become coated in ice. When they grow heavy enough, they begin to fall. If they pass through air that is warmer than freezing, they melt into raindrops before reaching the ground. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or other forms of frozen precipitation.

Raindrops do not usually begin as tiny, perfectly formed teardrops. Small droplets are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. As they fall and meet air resistance, larger drops flatten at the bottom. Very large drops become unstable and break apart into smaller ones, limiting how big a falling raindrop can get.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on conditions beneath the cloud. Falling drops may evaporate in dry air, leaving a streak called virga. If enough water survives the descent, it reaches the surface as rain. Wind can carry the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the cloud’s center.

After rain reaches the ground, it may soak into soil, collect in streams and lakes, or flow across the land into rivers and eventually the sea. Some returns to the air through evaporation or plant release. The cycle then continues: water rises, cools, condenses into clouds, and may fall again
